findings.title: Valid backup code alone can authenticate without the account password
findings.body: In the credentials authorize() the password check is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121), i.e. the password is skipped whenever any non-empty totpCode is supplied. The new backup-code branch at line 131 then runs when `credentials.backupCode` is set, without ever verifying the password. So a request containing email, an arbitrary junk totpCode (e.g. "000000"), and a valid backupCode signs the user in with no password knowledge. Backup codes are single-use 40-bit hex strings typically saved in plaintext files or on paper; they are intended as a second factor, not a password substitute. The server should require a verified password (or otherwise ensure the first-factor step actually happened) before accepting a backup code.

findings.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write; codes can be replayed or burned
findings.body: The backup code is consumed by reading `user.backupCodes`, decrypting, nulling the matched index, and writing the whole array back with an unconditional `prisma.user.update`. There is no transaction or conditional update, so two concurrent login requests presenting the same code can both pass `indexOf` and both succeed — the code is effectively reusable within the race window. Additionally, the code is burned inside authorize() before the rest of the sign-in pipeline completes; if anything fails downstream or the client never receives the success response (network drop), the user's code is permanently consumed and their retry with the same code returns IncorrectBackupCode. Consumption should be atomic (e.g. a conditional update filtered on the code being present, or a transaction with a re-check) and ideally only committed once sign-in is assured.

findings.title: Backup code comparison is case- and whitespace-sensitive, but codes are lowercase hex
findings.body: Backup codes are generated with `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` (lowercase a-f0-9), and verification does `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` with no lowercasing or trimming (same in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61). Codes can contain the letters a–f, so a user who types or saves the code in uppercase (the UI placeholder "XXXXX-XXXXX" actively suggests uppercase), or pastes it with leading/trailing whitespace, will be told the code is incorrect even though it is valid. Given each failed attempt is a dead end for the user, the input should be normalized (trim + toLowerCase) before comparison.

findings.title: "Generate backup codes in your settings" is impossible — no regeneration path exists, and pre-PR 2FA users have none
findings.body: The new `missing_backup_codes` message says "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no endpoint or UI to generate/regenerate backup codes — they are only created once, during initial 2FA setup (setup.ts), and only shown once. Users who enabled 2FA before this PR have `backupCodes = null`, so if they lose their authenticator the "Lost access" flow is a dead end, and users who dismiss the backup-codes dialog without saving can never retrieve their codes again. The error message instructs them to do something that cannot be done, on both the login page and the disable-2FA modal.

findings.title: resetState() does not clear the totpCode form field, leaving stale code from a previous setup
findings.body: resetState() clears password, errorMessage, and step, but never resets the react-hook-form `totpCode` field. After a completed (or abandoned) setup, the form still holds the previously entered 6-digit code. When the user later re-opens the modal and reaches the EnterTotpCode step, the registered hidden `totpCode` input still contains the old value while the digit boxes render empty; submitting (or any change that retriggers the auto-submit effect watching `totpCode`) can send the stale, now-invalid code, producing a confusing "code is incorrect" error before the user has typed anything. resetState should also call form.setValue("totpCode", "").

findings.title: onEnable is only fired from the "Close" button; dismissing the dialog via X/Escape skips it and resetState
findings.body: The prop contract says onEnable is "Called when the user enables two-factor auth", and previously it was invoked as soon as enable succeeded. Now it is only called from the backup-codes "Close" button click handler. If the user dismisses the dialog through the built-in close affordances (X button, Escape key, overlay click — all routed to onOpenChange), onEnable never fires, so any parent that refreshes its state in onEnable (e.g. the two-factor switch on the security settings page) will keep showing 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled. resetState is also skipped, leaving the modal on the DisplayBackupCodes step with the codes still in memory if reopened.

findings.title: Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of a one-way hash
findings.body: Backup codes are persisted as AES-encrypted plaintext (`symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes))`) using the shared CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and returned in plaintext in the API response. Unlike the TOTP secret (which must be recoverable to validate codes), backup codes can be validated by hashing the user input and comparing digests, which is the industry standard (GitHub, Google, etc.). As stored, anyone with database access plus the encryption key — a key already used for many other secrets — recovers all unused backup codes, which per the finding above can even be replayed as a standalone credential.

findings.title: No test covers actually using a backup code to log in or disable 2FA
findings.body: The PR's headline feature — authenticating with a backup code — has zero test coverage. The updated e2e tests only exercise the backup-codes screen's download/copy/close buttons; the TODO at the top of the file ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") acknowledges this. Neither the happy path (correct code logs in and is consumed), nor wrong-code rejection, nor code-single-use behavior is verified anywhere, leaving the new authorize() and disable.ts branches untested.

findings.title: tabIndex={-1} on the password visibility toggle removes keyboard access
findings.body: The change adds `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button inside PasswordField. This makes the toggle unreachable via keyboard (Tab/Synth events), so keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer reveal their password on the login page, the 2FA setup modal, or anywhere else PasswordField is used. If this was added to keep e2e selectors stable, it should be scoped differently rather than disabling focus for all users.

findings.title: Users on the external TOTP login path (totpEmail) have no way to use a backup code
findings.body: When a user arrives at /auth/login via a `totp` JWT (SSO/Google users with 2FA who were redirected by loginWithTotp), the footer rendered is ExternalTotpFooter, which only offers a "cancel" button — the "Lost access" button that switches to the BackupCode input exists only in TwoFactorFooter. Such users have backup codes generated by this feature but no UI to enter them, so if they lose their authenticator they are locked out despite the feature existing. The lost-access toggle should also be offered in the external TOTP flow.
